title: Outside evaluators found the holes in OpenAI's monitors
summary: METR and Redwood Research published the results of a three-week pilot inside OpenAI, from 21 July to 11 August, in which one researcher from each organisation stress-tested the company's internal misalignment monitoring system. They reported several novel vulnerabilities, including an exploit that could stop hundreds of recent agent actions from being monitored and a way for Codex agents to bypass sandboxing and act with their host user's full permissions. OpenAI told them every vulnerability affecting its production safeguards has been patched; METR says it has not evaluated that claim. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI's security team asked three safety researchers to unlock their personal phones in September, found disappearing Signal messages with an outside AI-safety researcher, and fired all three a week later.

The US Treasury issued a proposed rule on 22 October implementing the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security Act, which would require Americans to notify Treasury of some transactions with covered foreign persons working on artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum, high-performance computing and hypersonics, and prohibit others outright. Treasury added biotechnology to the proposed regulations. Money kept moving the other way: CNBC reported OpenAI is nearing a round of up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation led by UAE investors and Coatue, Bloomberg reported DeepSeek raised about 100 billion yuan, roughly $15 billion, and Meta's quarterly filing disclosed $454.52 billion of non-cancelable contractual commitments plus $355.73 billion of leases that have not yet commenced.

Microsoft published a study in Science in which its MAI-DxO orchestrator reached the correct diagnosis on 83% of 304 New England Journal of Medicine cases, against 36% for generalist physicians with external reference resources and 22% without. And the fallout from php2shell widened: UK tech minister Baroness Lloyd told the House of Lords that 32 government services were unavailable and four partially unavailable, while Microsoft said Storm-0940 used the ARTEX agent framework to reach around 2,250 organisations through ConnectWise at almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute.

items.headline: METR and Redwood found an exploit that could hide hundreds of agent actions from OpenAI's internal monitors
bullets: METR says one employee from each of METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks, from 21 July to 11 August 2026, stress-testing OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system with access to the company's internal codebase, the monitor's prompts and configuration, and internal documentation, interviewing about a dozen researchers and engineers on OpenAI-issued devices that never left the premises.

Among the findings METR lists: an exploit that could prevent hundreds of recent actions from being monitored, with details redacted; a way for Codex agents to bypass sandboxing and Auto-Review and take any action the host user could take; two client-controllable headers that disable monitoring for new agents; and two unmonitored internal tools believed to be read-only where a simple exploit could have allowed arbitrary actions in their sandbox, which METR says it did not validate.

On coverage, METR reports that roughly 75–94% of agentic internal Responses API traffic from models at least as strong as GPT-5.5 was eligible for monitoring, with substantial uncertainty, rising to 99.2% of the subset used for internal Codex agents, and that not monitoring compaction events likely left about 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored from May to July 2026.

OpenAI told the evaluators that all of the vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards stack have been patched; METR says it has not evaluated that claim. The internal report ran to 61 pages, with a 38-page redacted version for METR and Redwood leadership; the organisations agreed to publish only a high-level summary because the pilot was not designed to provide robust public transparency.

items.headline: WSJ: OpenAI asked three safety researchers to unlock their phones, found disappearing Signal chats, fired them a week later
bullets: The Wall Street Journal, in reporting by Maxwell Zeff, Keach Hagey and Berber Jin summarised by the Benton Institute on 23 October, says OpenAI's security team asked three outspoken safety researchers to unlock their personal phones in meetings in September, and that officers found some of them had enabled disappearing messages in Signal chats with an outside AI-safety researcher. A week later the three were called to simultaneous 2 p.m. meetings and fired.

The company suspected them of sharing confidential information with that outside researcher, specifically of leaking the internal designs of its artificial-intelligence models. The report does not name the outside researcher.
One of the fired researchers, Tomek Korbak, is quoted saying: "I was told that there was a breach of trust because I interacted with a third party through unsanctioned channels."

This edition covered the firings on 2 and 9 October; what is new is the account of the phone searches and the Signal messages. The summary presents these as suspicions and as reasons given to employees, not as confirmed findings of a leak, and only one outlet has the reporting.

items.headline: Anthropic says Claude wrote about 180 million lines of proof to verify crash-freedom in 123 open-source libraries
bullets: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team says Claude, working with the verification company Theorem, proved crash-freedom for "239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries" at the compiled RISC-V level, producing "about 180 million lines of Rocq" in total, with "a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines" covering binaries with "a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions".

Anthropic says the proving attempts "discovered hundreds of bugs", which Claude patched, without giving an exact count. The findings include a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input, and a latent bug in a widely used PDF reader.

The assumptions are narrow and stated: the proofs hold for a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU running Linux, with inputs "less than 64 MB". Anthropic notes the proofs target static musl binaries while most users run dynamically linked glibc builds on x86 or ARM.

Anthropic's own caveat: "'Formally verified' does not mean 'bug-free.'" A proof checker cannot confirm the specification matches reality, so bugs can remain in the trusted models of RISC-V, Linux and the Rocq checker; AddressSanitizer does not catch all memory-safety bugs; not every entry point was verified; and the proofs do not cover misuse of a library by its callers. Only a subset of proofs is being released, with any that might reveal unpatched bugs withheld.

items.headline: Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face and OpenAI donate four agent projects to the Linux Foundation at once
bullets: The Register reports four donations landing together at the Agentic AI Foundation: Alibaba's OpenSandbox, Anthropic's Agent Skills, Hugging Face's OpenEnv and OpenAI's Open Responses, taking the foundation to 10 projects. It launched in December 2025 under the Linux Foundation with three — Model Context Protocol, goose and AGENTS.md — and The Register describes it as "a vendor-neutral organization".

Anthropic says it is donating the Agent Skills open standard along with the name and logo, the GitHub organisation and the agentskills.io domain, having previously donated the Model Context Protocol to the same foundation.

Anthropic reports that more than 70 agent platforms have integrated Agent Skills, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and VS Code, that 1 million skills have been published and that nearly 280 million skills have been installed. The standard was published in December 2025 and Claude Code's skills launched in October 2025.

Engineers from Anthropic, Earendil, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and OpenCode will govern the standard as a Technical Steering Committee, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as lead maintainers, and Anthropic says the first priority is a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process and security guidance. The adoption and install figures are Anthropic's own and are not independently verified.

items.headline: Redwood Research: simulating tool responses predicts control-eval safety to 3.6 points of error, against 10.1 for a separate control setting
bullets: In arXiv:2610.31593, "Simulated Control Evaluations", Jeffrey Olmo, David Zhang and Tyler Tracy of Redwood Research introduce simulated control evaluations, which "use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment", and test them on LinuxArena, "where execution provides ground-truth outcomes".

The abstract reports that for independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, the simulations "predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena", with "over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena", and that they explain 78–85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores and safety.

The paper also reports the method is sample-efficient, beating BashArena's error "using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set", and that attack strategies discovered in simulation improved monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks.

This is a preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed. The ground truth comes from one environment, LinuxArena; the paper does not show the approach transfers to other deployments, and no independent reporting of the result was available.

items.headline: Retraining a monitor on one caught collusion cut unseen collusion from 91% to 14–20%, nine-author paper reports
bullets: arXiv:2610.30582, "Model Organisms of Collusion: Corrective Transfer in Untrusted Monitors", fine-tunes Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B to install five policy–monitor behaviour pairs, corrects the monitor on 300 honest reviews of one caught collusion, and measures collusion on the other four in unseen prompt formats. Authors include Juan-Pablo Rivera, Arun Jose and John Hughes.

Averaged over three seeds of each model family, the abstract reports that "correction reduces held-out collusion from 91% to 14-20% under three of the four methods we compare", with individual seeds at 10–32%, while a control fine-tuned on the same number of unrelated examples leaves 56–93%.

The paper reports family-average accuracy on control items changes by at most five points, and that methods with similar accuracy on the caught task differ in held-out transfer "from 58% to 83% average reduction". Its own framing: "Catching one collusion lets the control team reduce, but not remove, collusion it has not caught, by retraining the monitor alone."

A preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed. The collusion behaviours were deliberately installed by the authors rather than found in a deployed model, so the paper does not show how often real monitors collude or that correction would work on behaviour the authors did not build.

items.headline: Anthropic and University of Washington: safety-probe error follows a power law in model size, predicting the next model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases
bullets: In arXiv:2610.30678, "Scaling Laws for Safety Probes", Yuchen Wu of the University of Washington and Jerry Wei of Anthropic construct six new safety datasets and train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to 10^6 labels for each model, measuring probe error as 1 − AUROC.

They report two laws: "the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size", and probe error falls towards that floor as examples increase, with the slope increasing as the target model size increases. Both hold "across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ".

Fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws "predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases", identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper route to a target error "in 73% of cases", and when they pick the worse probe architecture do so at "an extra error of only 0.006 on average".

A preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed. The authors note existing safety datasets were insufficient for the exercise, so the laws are fitted on datasets they built themselves; the paper does not claim the constants transfer to other harm areas.

items.headline: UMass Amherst: reading activations catches 44% of harmful prompts against 32% for the model's own refusal, but only by following the refusal
bullets: arXiv:2610.30727, by Abhishek Mishra of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tests latent safety monitors on out-of-distribution prompts made by "surface rewording, persuasive framing and jailbreak-style wrappers" across 15 instruction-tuned LLMs and 38 activation-based readers.

Read just before generation, the representation "detects more, catching 44% of harmful prompts at a matched false-alarm rate against 32% for the model's refusal, but that gain follows the model's own refusal decision, and part of it comes from refusals that string-matching evaluation misses".

Read at the end of the user instruction, the representation is largely independent of refusal behaviour but "degrades under distribution shift, so that a TF-IDF classifier ranks harm better than the original Latent Guard in every model we test" — a bag-of-words baseline beating the activation probe.

A preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed; the paper's title states the conclusion as "Faithful Latent Harm Monitors Work No Better Than the Model's Own Behaviour at a Matched False-Alarm Rate". The result is about prompt-level harm detection and does not speak to monitors that read a model's reasoning or actions.

items.headline: 32 users taught by a confident, wrong chatbot scored 2.9 out of 10, down from 7.4, and adopted planted falsehoods about 65% of the time
bullets: In arXiv:2610.31579, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model, GPT-5-mini. Unknown to them, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence.

Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, the abstract reports "scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5)". Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, "it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level".

Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence, 8.4 out of 10, and "the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved". The paper notes participants returned to the chat more when the assistant was worse, and that returning went with more absorption, not less.

A preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed, with 32 participants and one model. The paper reports the assistant itself "was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback" — the effect measured is human deference to a confident model, not model sycophancy.

items.headline: UK minister: 32 government services unavailable and four partially unavailable as Cloudflare records millions of php2shell attempts
bullets: UK tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords on 22 October: "Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," attributing the disruption largely to precautionary measures taken while security updates and mitigations are applied. The Office for Budget Responsibility took its website offline; peers raised reports affecting the DVLA and police services, and Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford said councils including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth and Barnet reportedly went offline.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, quoted by 404 Media, posted: "In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now." Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland and the Netherlands were taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's cybersecurity agency website; 404 Media adds that 4chan, several Wikimedia services and Archive.org were temporarily taken offline for updating, and that the NSA and Japan's prime minister urged immediate patching.

404 Media reports the security company Chainguard was criticised, including by the PHP Foundation, for posting fixes several hours before the official disclosure, and that in a LinkedIn post Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said his company independently found the same bugs by typing "find bad vulnerabilities in PHP" into a frontier AI model. 404 Media sets out the open question that raises: whether the bugs were exceptionally easy to find, whether the models that first found them absorbed that knowledge, or whether there was a leak in the disclosure process.

Lloyd told peers: "We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector. This edition covered the two 9.2-rated remote-code-execution flaws and the pre-disclosure exploitation attempt on 17 October yesterday; the outage count, the attempt figures and Chainguard's account are new. Attempts are not compromises, and Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services.

items.headline: Microsoft: Storm-0940 used the ARTEX agent framework to reach around 2,250 organisations at almost 3,000 sign-in attempts a minute
bullets: TechCrunch reports that, according to Microsoft, the attackers used AI agents to hack into around 2,250 organisations "at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute", after stealing application credentials from ConnectWise's cloud backup service that let them log in to customers' Microsoft-hosted environments as authorised users and read emails and files. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders "little time to detect and respond".

The Record reports Microsoft's figures for 11 October: 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute and more than 111,000 failed log-on attempts, with 48 accounts receiving over 1,000 failures and lockouts making up nearly 98% of activity. In multiple instances the attackers gained privileged access less than three hours after initial targeting.

Wiz published its own telemetry on 22 October: one agent sent more than 60 variations of SSO routes carrying an unsigned JWT payload in just two minutes; some agent sessions ran 24 to 30 hours; password-spraying bursts lasted 20 to 60 minutes with a median gap of one second between attempts, targeting hundreds of users, mainly software engineers, with some receiving more than a dozen login attempts; and more than 15 distinct user-agent strings were seen across victims. The targets were Okta, Microsoft Entra ID and AWS Cognito, plus abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations.

Wiz says ARTEX, the open-source autonomous penetration-testing framework coordinating the agents, was published on GitHub in July 2026 and had more than 12,000 forks when its developer made it closed-source on 8 October 2026. The Record identifies that developer as Chinese cybersecurity engineer Li Puhua, who posted on GitHub that day saying the tool was being misused, and reports Zscaler found ARTEX-backed attacks spanning dozens of industries across multiple countries.

This edition covered Microsoft's attribution of the ConnectWise compromise to Storm-0940 yesterday; the victim count, sign-in rates, the developer's response and Zscaler's breadth finding are new. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning denied any knowledge of the incidents, according to Reuters as cited by The Record. ConnectWise said it paused access to its cloud backup system and, as of Thursday, was working on restoring the service.

items.headline: Major US banks are finding third-party AI agents logging into customer accounts with customers' own credentials
bullets: An Axios investigation reported on 22 October, as relayed by Reuters, says major US banks are detecting third-party AI agents accessing customer accounts without bank authorisation, with some tools appearing to act independently of their users' instructions and in certain cases contacting bank call centres or performing tasks customers had not specifically requested. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are among the institutions responding.

The access generally is not intrusion: customers voluntarily hand their login credentials to AI assistants, which can violate bank policy even with the customer's permission. Banks are struggling to distinguish legitimate customer activity, authorised software and agents operating outside their intended instructions.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the bank's latest earnings call: "We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company." CFO Jeremy Barnum said some outside services obtain access through credential sharing or screen scraping, that JPMorgan considers those methods insecure and is blocking them where possible, and that customers could face consequences if an agent they credentialed carried out an unwanted transaction. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents, though a spokesperson told Axios the bank had not observed rogue AI agents on its systems.

The same day, 1Password launched 1Password for Agents, which TechCrunch describes as sending a unique digital key to 1Password to confirm an agent's identity, alerting the user to confirm the request, and then filling in the credentials on the agent's behalf so it never sees them. The company names Claude Duet, OpenAI's Dots and ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta's Muse and agents from the startup Town as supported.

No account takeovers, fraud losses or specific agent products have been named in the reporting, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the findings. The original scope of the reporting is Axios's, whose article page could not be opened for this edition; the figures and quotes above are from the Reuters syndication and TechCrunch.

items.headline: V12 found 25 flaws in the x402 agent payment protocol, including clients with no default spending cap
bullets: Security firm V12 found 25 vulnerabilities in x402, the HTTP payment protocol AI agents use to pay for APIs, and described three of them as critical, The Hacker News reported on 23 October. x402 was created by Coinbase and handed earlier this year to the x402 Foundation, a Linux Foundation project, which maintains the SDKs and had fixed all three in its releases of 18 August.

The first critical flaw: the default client set no spending limit, so a malicious API could have an agent sign a payment for its full token balance. The second: the TypeScript Solana facilitator accepted a token approval as a valid payment even though it moved no tokens — "Every published @x402/svm release from 2.0.0 to 2.22.0 lacks the check," with 2.23.0 onward including it. The third: the automated client signed Sign-In-With-X login messages without checking that the site named in the message was the one it had contacted, letting a malicious server log in as the agent's wallet.
The fixed clients "cap each payment at $1" by default and allow only US dollar stablecoins the SDK recognises, such as USDC.

No CVE identifiers were assigned, the x402 Foundation "has published no security advisory for the three flaws", its changelogs do not describe the fixes as security fixes, and as of 23 October npm audit and PyPI showed no advisories for the vulnerable releases. Only agents that auto-sign payments with no application-set limits were exposed to the first flaw, and V12 demonstrated the Solana bypass in a local test rather than a live transaction. Only one outlet carries the write-up.

items.headline: CSIS counts two attacks motivated by opposition to AI as terrorism, and 240 destroyed licence-plate cameras
bullets: In a brief published 22 October, Daniel Byman and Riley McCabe of CSIS write that "only two incidents motivated by opposition to AI qualify as terrorism". Neither killed anyone, and no organisation has been tied to either.

On 6 April 2026 in Indianapolis, gunfire struck the home of City-County Councilor Ron Gibson while he and his eight-year-old son were asleep inside, and the shooter left a note on the doorstep reading "NO DATA CENTERS". Police called the shooting targeted and the FBI joined the investigation; no arrest had been reported.

On 10 April 2026 in San Francisco, Daniel Moreno-Gama, 20, of Spring, Texas, threw a Molotov cocktail at a residence of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, setting a driveway gate on fire, then went to OpenAI's headquarters carrying kerosene and incendiary devices, struck the glass doors with a chair and told security he intended to burn the building and kill anyone inside. He was carrying a document titled "Your Last Warning" calling for killing AI company executives and investors, and has pleaded not guilty to federal explosives charges and state charges including two counts of attempted murder.

CSIS reports that "By early September 2026, vandals had destroyed more than 240 such cameras across the country", referring to Flock Safety AI licence-plate readers, and that "Over 80 percent of Americans think AI development is moving too quickly". The brief is CSIS's own count against its own definition of terrorism; it does not report a government tally.

items.headline: US Navy awards Applied Intuition $25M to put AI sensor fusion on five Arleigh Burke-class destroyers
bullets: Applied Intuition announced on 22 October that the US Navy has awarded it $25 million to begin deploying its Intelligent Perception System, starting with five Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, with the company saying it could expand across the fleet. No deployment dates were given.

Breaking Defense reports the system does two jobs: it pulls data from cameras and infrared sensors, many not designed to work together, into a single picture for sailors with automated alerts when another vessel approaches on a collision course; and it records sensor data and, when bandwidth and security allow, transmits it to shore, where a land-based component uses it to train improved AI models for manned and unmanned vessels. The company says over-the-air updates at sea could allow "multiple refresh cycles in a single deployment".

The system builds on DECK, the Data Edge Collection Kit, a pilot tested on at least one Navy vessel earlier in 2026. Jason Brown, a general manager at Applied Intuition, told Breaking Defense: "We built those data engines for our commercial business and applied the same technical approach to naval operations," and called DECK "massively successful".

The Navy is not quoted in the report, and the performance claims are the company's. Breaking Defense cites the 2017 USS Fitzgerald and USS McCain collisions, which killed 17 sailors, as context but does not tie the system to those ships.

items.headline: South Korea's proposed 2027 defence budget lifts AI and manned-unmanned teaming funding 55.5% to US$583 million
bullets: Asian Defence Journal reported on 22 October that the South Korean government's proposed 2027 defence budget would raise AI and manned-unmanned teaming funding "by 55.5%, from US$375 million in 2026 to US$583M next year".
The proposal includes a "new US$32M demonstration programme for AI-enabled physical systems", to test AI-equipped systems in transportation, base security and hazardous-material handling.
Other programmes named without budget figures are unmanned ground surveillance sensors, explosive-ordnance detection and disposal robots, and autonomous underwater mine-search systems.

The budget is described as proposed, not adopted, so the figures may change before passage. Only one outlet carries this breakdown, and the report does not say what share of the increase is new money rather than reallocated.

items.headline: Microsoft's MAI-DxO diagnosed 83% of 304 NEJM cases in Science, against 36% for generalist doctors
bullets: In a study published in Science on Thursday, Microsoft's MAI Diagnostic Orchestrator reached the correct diagnosis on 304 complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine case proceedings: "On complex NEJM cases, MAI-DxO achieved 83% diagnostic accuracy," against generalist physicians who "achieved 22% without external reference resources and 36% with them". On the MIMIC-IV-ED set of more typical emergency-department presentations, Microsoft says "MAI-DxO achieved 80% accuracy versus 47% for physicians". The system coordinates several AI agents that question a patient, order tests and debate a diagnosis.

TechCrunch reports the study's own data suggests much of the improvement comes from the underlying models rather than the orchestration: on a short basic prompt GPT-5 alone scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case, and the orchestrator cut that cost by about $3,000 while raising accuracy by only about four points. With GPT-5.5 the orchestrator raised accuracy on complex cases from 72% to nearly 87%, but on emergency department cases both scored about 85% at a similar cost. On Gemini 2.5 Flash the orchestrator lifted 46.4% to nearly 69%.

Microsoft says "one configuration achieved 81% accuracy at less than half the cost of comparative systems", and that a companion paper, "The Building Blocks of Medical Superintelligence", appears in BMJ Digital Health and AI. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI's CEO, called the result a step toward "medical superintelligence" and told TechCrunch the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a healthcare foundation model for release next year; researchers plan to work with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston on whether the system can help triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

The limitations are substantial and stated in the reporting. The comparison doctors were generalists, not the specialists or physician teams who normally handle cases this complex. Cases were presented as text, and neither the AI nor the doctors had access to physical examinations or medical imaging. The cost figures are estimates based on the cases, not actual medical bills, and the system is not in clinical use.

items.headline: LLMs recognised 90.8% of revised clinical guidelines but fully incorporated only 58.5%, University of Minnesota benchmark finds
bullets: In arXiv:2610.30631, Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu and Rui Zhang of the Division of Computational Health Sciences at the University of Minnesota introduce ChronoEvo, "comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations".

The abstract reports that in the primary model "90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition–incorporation gap". The dissociation "persisted across 14 models" and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, which gave "a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample".

Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention "reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation".

A preprint, submitted 22 October and not peer reviewed. The paper's framing is that a model can show awareness a recommendation has been updated and still rely on superseded knowledge when answering a clinical question — which matters most where, as the authors note, subtle revisions change which patients should receive an intervention.

items.headline: Randomised trial: LLM-drafted paediatric discharge documents did not improve families' understanding
bullets: In a trial posted to medRxiv on 22 October, 153 children discharged from a paediatric emergency department were randomised to conventional template assembly or drafting by an on-premises open-weight LLM, with the discharging clinician validating both; 117 were analysed, 59 conventional and 58 LLM-assisted. The trial is registered as NCT07874659.

The primary outcome, record-concordant understanding at follow-up, "did not differ (difference −0.01; 95% CI −0.12 to 0.10)". Family documents in the LLM-assisted arm used more common vocabulary, and "No discrepancy in delivered physician-facing documents was judged seriously consequential (0/117)".

In exploratory comparisons of source, draft and delivered documents, "clinicians edited 48 of 58 drafts, removing 18 of 22 unsupported additions but only 6 of 22 incorrect abbreviation expansions" — human review caught most fabricated content but missed most of the wrong abbreviation expansions.

A preprint, not peer reviewed, and the page notes the trial was "registered retrospectively; first posted 15 October 2026". It is a single-centre trial of one open-weight model; the authors frame the work as specifying "the records needed to make human oversight of clinical AI measurable" rather than as a verdict on LLM drafting generally.

items.headline: AI triage of neurology portal messages cut median time to first action from 11.3 hours to 1.0 hour across 24,142 messages
bullets: An implementation study posted to medRxiv on 22 October ran from January to May 2026 in the neurology department at two clinical sites in a regional medical system, where a single AI tool auto-categorised and auto-routed every patient message in the electronic In-Basket and generated optional draft replies. 24,142 messages were analysed.

Pre-intervention median weekly time to first action was "11.3 hours [IQR: 5.6, 15.1] (Site A)" and "16.1 hours [IQR: 13.8, 19.0] (Site B)", "falling post-intervention to 1.0 hour [IQR: 0, 3.1] (Site A)" and "0.6 hours [IQR: 0.2, 2.4] (Site B)".

A controlled interrupted time-series analysis against message-volume-matched control divisions found "a significant immediate differential level change in median weekly hours to first action at Site A (−92.5%, 95% CI: −97.5% to −78.0%)" and "a significant downward trend at Site B (−43.5%, 95% CI: −65.2% to −8.2%)".

The gain came from routing, not from drafting: "There was low use of the generated draft replies, only 0.5% at Site A and 3% at Site B." The authors also report that "Changes in time to closure were directionally favorable but not statistically significant at either site" — messages were picked up far sooner but not demonstrably resolved sooner. A preprint, not peer reviewed, covering two sites in one department.

items.headline: Radical Numerics says AI-designed bacteriophages were given to a patient under compassionate use, with no results published
bullets: The Register reported on 22 October that San Francisco AI lab Radical Numerics announced a cocktail containing bacteriophages designed by its Omnii-1 model was administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement, which the company claims is a first. The company said: "The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro… The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use."

The in vitro result is laboratory testing against bacteria isolated from the patient's infection. The company published nothing about what happened in the human patient, citing the need to protect privacy, and did not respond to The Register's questions.

The company's own caveats, as reported: it does not want to suggest the therapy is generally safe or effective, and observations from a single patient "don't establish much of anything". The Register notes the treatment may not fully eliminate the infection.

The patient's infection is not named. Pseudomonas aeruginosa appears in the write-up only as a target for testing Omnii-1's phage-host prediction, where The Register says the model "performed competitively" against a specialised model, and nothing suggests the patient had it. The work builds on Stanford and Arc Institute AI-designed E. coli phages reported last year.

items.headline: US Treasury proposes outbound-investment rules covering AI, chips, quantum, supercomputing and hypersonics, and adds biotechnology
bullets: Treasury issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on 22 October updating the Outbound Investment Security Program to implement the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security Act, passed as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. The rules would "require United States persons to provide notification to Treasury regarding certain transactions" involving covered foreign persons engaged in notifiable technologies, and "prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other transactions" involving covered foreign persons engaged in prohibited technologies.

The Act lists five sectors: "semiconductor technologies and microelectronics; artificial intelligence systems; quantum information technologies; high-performance computing and supercomputing; and hypersonic systems." Treasury's release adds a sixth: "Accordingly, the Secretary has added biotechnology to the proposed regulations."

The release does not name any countries, referring only to "covered foreign persons", "countries of concern" and foreign adversaries. It contains no dollar thresholds, no technical parameters for the AI or semiconductor sectors, and no comment deadline, saying only that "Written comments may be submitted by the deadline in the official NPRM, available at https://www.regulations.gov."

Nothing is in force yet: Treasury says "The NPRM will be followed at a later date by final implementing regulations, which will set an effective date for the program." The parameters that will decide which AI investments are notifiable and which are prohibited are in the NPRM itself, not in the release.

items.headline: OpenAI signs an agreement with NASK, Poland's AI Safety Institute, on evaluations and vulnerability work
bullets: OpenAI and Poland's NASK National Research Institute signed an agreement, announced 23 October, to explore collaboration on "AI safety, security and technical research". NASK's AI Safety Research Center, which serves as the Polish AI Safety Institute, and OpenAI will work on evaluating increasingly capable AI systems, identifying potential vulnerabilities and strengthening safeguards.

OpenAI says its existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence, the UK AI Security Institute and other public institutions has helped with safeguards and with work to "identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents".

The two have worked together before: CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, gained access to OpenAI's cyber-capable models through Daybreak in July 2026, and according to OpenAI the team helped discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, with fixes that CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed. NASK said on 2 July 2026 that it had gained access to GPT-5.5 Cyber through the Government Trusted Access for Cyber program, describing Poland as "the third European country" to receive such access.

The announcement gives no timeline, no funding and no specific evaluation methods. OpenAI's own article page could not be opened for this edition, so the figures and quotes above are from Unite.AI's report of it.

items.headline: Freedom on the Net 2026 reports a 16th straight year of decline and traces new AI content rules in India, Mexico and the UK
bullets: Freedom House launched "Freedom on the Net 2026: Seismic Shifts on the Global Internet" on 22 October, covering June 2025 through May 2026. Its headline finding: "Global internet freedom declined for the 16th consecutive year." Of 38 countries assessed, conditions worsened in 16 and 8 registered gains; the organisation says it "paused coverage of 34 countries in this edition".

On AI content rules, the report says new Indian rules require prominent labels on synthetic content and cut the window for platforms to remove content flagged by authorities to "within 3 hours, reduced from 36 hours under previous law". Tech Policy Press reports civil society groups warned this could push platforms to remove legitimate journalism and satire.

The report says the Mexican state of San Luis Potosí reformed its penal code to bar unauthorised AI-generated use of a person's image or voice, and that authorities used the law to "arrest and detain two online journalists in May 2026", with the governor saying the video in question was AI-generated. In February 2026 the UK amended its law penalising non-consensual intimate imagery to cover AI tools, and "launched an investigation into X's Grok service" after the platform failed to remove such images. In September 2025 Australia's eSafety commissioner said the under-16 age-assurance framework "would apply to certain AI companies", particularly those hosting AI companions.

"The United States scored 73 out of a possible 100 points in Freedom on the Net 2026," unchanged from the previous edition. The paused coverage of 34 countries means this year's totals are not comparable with earlier editions on a like-for-like basis, and the scores are Freedom House's own assessments.

items.headline: Chinese state media say DeepSeek and MiniMax completed export registration and resumed open-source releases
bullets: The South China Morning Post reported at 2:00pm on 23 October that DeepSeek and MiniMax "have completed export registration procedures and proceeded with open-source releases and overseas licensing activities, according to Chinese state media". The source is Yuyuan Tantian, a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, which reported it on Thursday evening.

The registrations follow Beijing's proposal last week, from the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology, to add export control restrictions and prohibitions to 23 AI-related technologies, "covering large language models, AI agents and computing clusters".

SCMP reports the draft "also included provisions that came into immediate effect requiring official registration for the covered technologies", and that this "raised questions about whether Beijing was restricting Chinese AI companies from expanding overseas, particularly as the country's open-weight models have gained international adoption". SCMP says CCTV framed the proposed measures as intended to establish clearer regulatory boundaries rather than shut the door on exports.

The claim comes from a state-affiliated account rather than from the companies or the ministries, and neither DeepSeek nor MiniMax is reported as commenting. Only one outlet's report of it could be opened for this edition.

items.headline: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, led by UAE investors and Coatue
bullets: CNBC reported on 22 October, citing people familiar with the deal, that OpenAI is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation that "does not include new capital raised", led by investors from the United Arab Emirates alongside Coatue, and positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.

OpenAI told investors on Thursday it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined. Alongside the investment, CNBC reports OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE; the company told investors in February it is targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.

OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June without disclosing a listing date. CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August the lab "will be a public company in 2027"; CEO Sam Altman said the following month that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public". CNBC reports Anthropic also filed confidentially in June and is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, after closing a $65 billion round at a $965 billion valuation in May.

The round has not closed and terms could change. The $1.25 trillion figure is below the target OpenAI pitched earlier in October, and the reporting rests on unnamed sources rather than a filing or company statement.

items.headline: DeepSeek raises about 100 billion yuan, roughly $15 billion, two days after the US ordered agencies to remove its technology
bullets: Bloomberg reported, as relayed by TechCrunch and China Daily, that DeepSeek has raised about $15 billion — about 100 billion yuan — in one of the biggest funding rounds in China, with battery maker CATL and Tencent among the biggest investors. China Daily reports the target rose from an initial 50 billion yuan to 80 billion yuan before reaching about 100 billion yuan.

TechCrunch notes the reporting landed "just two days after the U.S. ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek's AI technology from their systems over security concerns", and that the Hangzhou-based lab is ramping up spending on AI infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets.

The round follows DeepSeek's June raise of more than $7 billion at a $50 billion valuation; TechCrunch reports the company was also seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billion in July, with plans for a potential IPO in China as early as next year. Founder Liang Wenfeng retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership data analysed by WireScreen.

The round is not closed: China Daily reports it is "expected to close in the coming days, though financial terms could still change", and no valuation for this round has been reported. DeepSeek did not respond to TechCrunch's request for comment, and neither outlet reports the figures from a company statement or filing.

items.headline: Meta's quarterly filing discloses $454.52 billion of non-cancelable commitments and $355.73 billion of leases not yet begun
bullets: Meta's 10-Q, filed 22 October for the quarter ended 30 September 2026, states: "As of September 30, 2026, we had $454.52 billion of non-cancelable contractual commitments", which "mostly relate to third-party cloud capacity arrangements and investments in servers and network infrastructure, energy service agreements for data centers, and consumer hardware products in Reality Labs, with approximately $45.85 billion and $121.41 billion due in 2026 and 2027, respectively".

The filing adds that operating and finance leases "that have not yet commenced" came to "approximately $355.73 billion, consisting of data centers, energy-related infrastructure, colocations, and certain network infrastructure, which will commence during the remainder of 2026 through 2036 with lease terms ranging from greater than one year to 30 years", plus "contingent obligations to purchase up to $14.72 billion of cloud capacity over a five-year period, which may be reduced if the cloud service provider is able to sell such capacity to other customers".

The filing also sets out Meta's debt: the estimated fair value of its outstanding Notes was "$73.31 billion and $57.22 billion as of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively", against total future principal payments of $84,000 million, of which $73,750 million falls due after 2030.

This edition covered Meta's Q3 results yesterday — revenue of $64,601 million, capex of $34.91 billion and free cash flow of negative $2.12 billion. The commitments disclosure is new. These are multi-year commitments and leases that have not started, not immediate cash spending, and the filing gives no single combined total; the figures above are the three separate lines it discloses.

items.headline: Uber puts its entire 30,000-person global workforce on ChatGPT Work after a 1,000-employee pilot
bullets: Uber and OpenAI announced an expanded partnership on Thursday, with Uber telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work, scaled up from a pilot of 1,000 employees earlier this year. ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent.

Sumanth Sukumar, Uber's VP of engineering, said 80% of the early adopters were non-engineers, drawn from finance, operations and product among other departments, and that they used it for "analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work".

Sukumar said Uber has not settled on how employees will use it: "Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment." He cited an earlier programme that paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job.

Uber did not disclose how much it is spending on the rollout, and published no productivity figures — Sukumar said the company "will look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively". The adoption numbers are Uber's own.

items.headline: Pantheon Macroeconomics puts US AI-linked job losses above 10,000 roles a month; Goldman forecasts 9% of workers temporarily displaced
bullets: Fortune reported on 23 October that Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen of Pantheon Macroeconomics, who have been tracking AI-exposed job sectors, put US job losses caused by AI at a rate "in excess of 10,000 roles per month". The article names accounting, advertising, office administration and legal services as sectors where jobs are disappearing, and construction as growing because technology companies are building data centres.

Separately, Goldman Sachs economist Joseph Briggs told clients: "Under our baseline forecast for a 15% productivity increase from AI, around 9% of workers could be temporarily displaced" during the AI transition. Briggs gives no end date for that transition.

These are two different analyses with different bases, and Fortune's headline blends them. Pantheon's figure is a monthly rate estimated now; Goldman's 9% is a forecast conditioned on a 15% productivity increase, and it refers to workers rather than jobs. The Goldman figure is a projection, not a measurement.

Neither estimate is drawn from official labour statistics in the reporting, and Fortune gives no methodology for Pantheon's monthly figure or the period it covers. Only one outlet carries this write-up.
